data.title: Week 1 — The Subject Matter of History
data.subtitle: Understanding history as a science and academic discipline

narr: Now let's dive into week one, which explores the fundamental nature of history as both a science and an academic discipline.
This week addresses key questions about what history is, its nature, its types and auxiliary disciplines, and how historians verify information reliability.
All the propositions, questions, tests, and terms for this week are based on the lecture materials and slides.

data.heading: Key Points: The Definition of History
bullets: History is the study of society's life in the past in all its aspects
Connected with the present and expectations of the future
The story of man in time, based on evidence
Evidence/fact is the "raw material" of history
History is an attempt to re-think the past: what happened, when, and how

narr: Let's explore the fundamental definition of history as presented in this week's materials.
History encompasses the study of human society throughout time, examining all aspects of life in the past.
It connects the past with our present and future expectations, helping us understand how we got here.
At its core, history is the story of humanity across time, built upon evidence and facts.
These facts serve as the raw material that historians use to reconstruct and interpret the past.
Ultimately, history represents our collective attempt to make sense of what happened, when it happened, and how it unfolded.

data.heading: Purpose of Historical Study

narr: The purpose of studying history extends beyond simple knowledge of the past.
It helps us understand the modern social, political, religious, and economic conditions that shape our world today.
Without historical knowledge, we lack the foundation for comprehending religion, customs, institutions, and systems of governance.
History reveals the cause-and-effect connections between past events and present circumstances.
This understanding enables us to analyze national and international issues with greater accuracy and objectivity.

data.heading: Propositions 1-4
bullets: The study of the present in the light of the past: the present has grown out of the past; causal connections are restored.
History is the science of man: the story of man's struggle through the ages, of how man learned to use and control his environment.
History is concerned with man in time: every event takes place at a definite moment of time, time gives perspective.
History is concerned with man in space: the interaction of man and his environment; politics, society, the economy and culture grow out of the geographical context.

narr: The first proposition establishes history as a way to understand the present by examining its roots in the past and the causal connections that shape our world today.
Secondly, history is essentially the story of humanity itself - our struggles, adaptations, and efforts to control our environment throughout time.
Thirdly, history places human events within specific timeframes, giving us perspective on when things happened and their sequence.
Finally, history examines how humans interact with their physical environment, showing how geography influences political, social, economic, and cultural developments.

data.heading: Propositions 5-8
bullets: An objective record of events: the data are built on primary sources and freed from subjective interpretation.
Many-sidedness: historical events cover all sides of life, not only the political one.
History is a dialogue between the events of the past and the gradually emerging ends of the future; on the basis of general attempts are made to forecast the future.
Not only narration but also analysis: causal connections are uncovered, general laws are formulated and compared with other societies.

narr: Fifth, history aims to be an objective record of events, built on primary sources and freed from subjective interpretation as much as possible.
Sixth, history recognizes the many-sidedness of human experience - it covers all aspects of life, not just political events.
Seventh, history serves as a dialogue between past events and future possibilities, helping us forecast future developments based on patterns.
Eighth, history goes beyond simply telling stories to include analysis, uncovering causal connections and formulating general laws that can be compared across different societies.

data.heading: Propositions 9-11
bullets: Continuity and coherence are the necessary conditions of history: human progress is handed down from generation to generation.
Relevance: only events important for the understanding of modern life are included.

All-comprehensiveness: history is not limited to one period, one country or one nation and embraces the political, social, economic, religious, literary, aesthetic and physical sides of life — a sense of world unity.

narr: Ninth, history recognizes that continuity and coherence are essential - human progress builds upon knowledge passed down through generations.
Tenth, history focuses on relevance, including only those events that help us understand modern life.
Finally, history is all-comprehensive, not limited by time, place, or nation, embracing all aspects of human experience and giving us a sense of world unity.

data.heading: Three Key Points
bullets: Experience — a combination of positive and negative notions about man or the historical process, their analysis and interpretation.
Thought — an idea or a point of view formed out of many facts: a preponderance of negative facts forms a negative thought, and vice versa.
Fact/Evidence — the raw material of history: the study of what happened, when and how.

narr: First, experience combines our positive and negative notions about people or historical events, along with their analysis and interpretation.
Second, thought refers to ideas or viewpoints formed from many facts - where an abundance of negative facts might lead to negative conclusions, and vice versa.
Third, facts or evidence serve as the raw material of history - they're what actually happened, when it happened, and how it happened.

data.heading: The Most Important Conclusion
bullets: Contrary to common opinion, the most important thing is EXPERIENCE, then thought, and only then fact.
The knowledge of many facts by itself does not mean the knowledge of history: without facts history turns into literature, but facts are merely instruments leading to reality.

narr: Here's a crucial insight that challenges common assumptions: experience is actually more important than thought, which is more important than facts.
Simply knowing many facts doesn't constitute understanding history. Without facts, history becomes literature, but facts themselves are just tools that help us reach historical understanding.

data.heading: Problem 1 — The Danger of Single Sources
data.problem: How can a single historical document distort our understanding of events?

steps.text: A document in the Samarkand archive shows a petitioner complaining to a qadi against his brother for not dividing paternal land.
This initial document might lead us to label the brother as 'bad'.
However, a second document reveals the brother offered his brother half the value of the land so he could buy land elsewhere or take up trade.
The income from the land was sufficient for only one family.

data.result: Multiple sources create a more objective picture; one source can significantly distort our understanding.

narr: Let's consider an example that illustrates why relying on single sources can be problematic.
In the Samarkand archive, there's a document where someone petitions a qadi against their brother for not dividing paternal land.
At first glance, this might make the brother seem like a bad person.
But when we examine a second document, we discover the brother offered his sibling half the land's value so he could buy land elsewhere or pursue trade.
The key insight here is that the land's income could support only one family.
This example demonstrates how multiple sources create a more objective picture, while a single source can significantly distort our understanding.

data.heading: The Interpretant's Influence
bullets: "History is written by the victors" — governments and funds pay for the writing of history and want it presented in ways they imagine.
Historians often depended on rulers for support, affecting their perspectives.
It's necessary to compare different data from different sources to get a more complete picture.

narr: There's a saying that "history is written by the victors" — this reflects how those in power often influence historical narratives.
Governments and funding sources pay for historical research and often want it presented in ways that align with their vision.
Historians historically depended on rulers for support, which could affect their perspectives and conclusions.
This is why comparing different data from various sources is essential to developing a more complete and objective understanding.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Changing Interpretations Over Time
data.problem: How does the interpretation of historical figures change depending on the political context?

steps.text: Amir Timur (Timur) was studied mostly negatively under Soviet rule due to ideological influences.
In the years of independence, his status was raised to that of a national hero.
Research showed that Timur developed trade, architecture, international relations and science.
Similarly, Genghis Khan is viewed as a barbarian conqueror in some contexts but as a hero by Mongols.

data.result: The assessment of historical figures depends heavily on the position and perspective of the interpreter.

narr: Let's look at how interpretations of historical figures change over time based on political contexts.
Under Soviet rule, Amir Timur was studied mostly negatively due to ideological influences.
However, after independence, his status was elevated to that of a national hero.
Research revealed that Timur actually contributed to trade, architecture, international relations, and science.
Similarly, Genghis Khan is often portrayed as a barbaric conqueror who destroyed flourishing cities, but for Mongols, he's a hero.
This example clearly shows how our assessment of historical figures depends heavily on the position and perspective of the interpreter.

data.heading: Knowing vs. Doing History
bullets: "Knowing history" — the accumulation of information, "walking encyclopedias", collectors of facts "in a cupboard of knowledge".
"Doing history" — interrogating the past in order to make sense of the world; historical research and historical thinking.
"Doing history" involves working with competing versions and narratives, understanding "strangers in time", even if they are not strangers in space.

narr: There's an important distinction between "knowing history" and "doing history".
Knowing history is simply the accumulation of information, like being a walking encyclopedia or a collector of facts stored away.
Doing history, however, involves actively interrogating the past to make sense of our world through research and historical thinking.
When we "do history", we work with competing versions and narratives, trying to understand people who might be "strangers in time", even if we share the same physical space.

data.heading: Archaeology
bullets: The scientific study of material remains of past human life: from stone tools to modern discarded objects.
From dwellings, temples and tombs to palaces and pyramids.
The word comes from the Greek archaia ("antiquities") + logos ("teaching").
Archaeologists first describe and classify finds, then place them in historical context.
Over 150 years of excavations in Central Asia have revealed the region's way of life, origins, trade, and economy.

narr: Archaeology is the scientific study of material remains from past human life, ranging from ancient stone tools to modern discarded objects.
Archaeologists examine everything from dwellings, temples, and tombs to palaces and pyramids.
The term comes from the Greek words archaia meaning "antiquities" and logos meaning "teaching".
While archaeologists begin by describing and classifying finds, their main goal is to place these material remains in their proper historical context.
For over 150 years, extensive local and international excavations in Central Asia have revealed much about the region's way of life, origins, trade, and economy.

data.heading: Ethnography and Ethnology

Ethnographers use participant observation: studying a group by taking part in its activities.
Ethnological research acts as an "intellectual antivirus" of society, cleansing it of rumors and superstitions.

narr: Ethnography and ethnology come from the Greek words ethnos meaning "people" and graphein meaning "to write".
According to Wolcott, ethnography involves describing the "ordinary social behaviors" of recognizable groups of people.
Ethnographers often use the method of participant observation, where they study a group by actually taking part in its activities.
Ethnological research serves as an "intellectual antivirus" for society, helping to cleanse it of rumors and superstitions.

narr: Source studies operate on the principle of "trust but verify" when examining historical documents.
This field determines the authenticity of information and examines the behavior and background of the author.
Source studies analyze the language used in the document, its character, and writing style.
It recognizes that language evolves over time, with words changing their meaning or even falling out of use completely.

data.heading: Historiography
bullets: The study of how historians develop history as an academic discipline.
Examines any body of historical work on a particular subject.
Examples include the historiography of the Central Asian renaissance, World War II, the Middle Ages, and early Islam.
Since the 19th century, a historiographical literature has developed, raising questions about the influence of historians' loyalties.

narr: Historiography is the study of how historians develop history as an academic discipline itself.
It examines any body of historical work focused on a particular subject or time period.
Examples include the historiography of the Central Asian renaissance, World War II, the Middle Ages, and early Islam.
Since the 19th century, as academic history developed, a substantial historiographical literature has emerged, raising important questions about how historians' loyalties might influence their work.

narr: Historical sources are broadly categorized as primary or secondary.
Primary sources are documents or artifacts created by witnesses or participants during the period under study.
These include manuscripts, archival materials, books, data, maps, objects, oral history, and various printed materials.
Secondary sources are created considerably later by people who weren't participants, and they often analyze primary sources without reproducing them verbatim.

narr: The historian's toolkit includes source criticism and synthesis.
Source criticism involves evaluating the quality, validity, reliability, and relevance of sources.
Historians ask five key questions about each source: when it was created, where it was created, by whom, from what original material, and in what original form.
Synthesis involves historical reasoning with emphasis on objectivity, causality, chronology, and context.

The Soviet system applied principles of 'language nationalism,' defining territories by language and supposed common history. Uzbekistan set apart the Karakalpak Autonomous Republic for a different language, and Tajikistan established Badakhshan as an autonomous region.

The Soviet government promoted Turkic languages and Tajik as modern languages, ensured universal literacy, and implemented 'korenizatsiya'—the preferment of local cadres in party and state structures. This nation-building occurred both from above and below but without true sovereignty, under the ideological homogenization of the CPSU.

narr: In the early Soviet period, the USSR established a legal framework for Uzbekistan's sovereignty. The 1924 constitution proclaimed the voluntary principle of the federal structure, while the 1927 constitution declared Uzbekistan an equal-in-rights and sovereign component.

Fayzulla Khodjayev led the government, working to advance local interests. During 1924-1928, the share of Uzbeks in central organs grew from 23% to 32.3%, and by the end of 1930, reached 75% at lower levels of state apparatus.

During this period, Uzbekistan existed as a raw-material appendage. The centuries-old dynastic statehood was replaced by 'nation-building' states that sowed ethnic conflicts, with characteristics including repression, the cult of personality, and the absence of private entrepreneurship.

By 1933, more than 5,500 kulak families had been deported beyond the republic, and during the 'cleansing' of kolkhozes, over 60,000 more dehkans were repressed.

data.heading: The Four Phases of Soviet Repression in Uzbekistan

narr: Now, let's examine the four phases of Soviet repression in Uzbekistan, which represent critical periods of political oppression.
Phase 1, from the 1920s to early 1930s, involved the rollback from the NEP and targeted the national intelligentsia and politicians advocating alternative forms of development.
Phase 2, from 1936-1939 known as the Great Terror, saw fabricated cases against leadership including Fayzulla Khodjayev and others. By spring 1938, over 70% of republican leaders had been repressed.
Phase 3, from 1946-1953, continued repression against the intelligentsia, financiers, and war participants until Stalin's death.
Phase 4, from 1983-1985, known as the Cotton or Uzbek Affair, was a campaign against corruption that led to the arrest of over 25,000 leaders and economic managers.

September 1 was declared Independence Day.
